newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy ready to take more budget pain for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Italy ready to take more budget pain for EMU.

text.p: The Italian government signalled at the weekend it was prepared to swallow more bitter budgetary medicine this year to ensure it becomes a founder member of the single European currency.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi said more austerity measures were likely in the coming months although he wanted to see key state accounts before deciding, while Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said the government was ready to act.
But central bank governor Antonio Fazio warned that Italy could not take any more taxes in its last gasp efforts to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Prodi told reporters in the northern city of Bologna on Sunday that Italy was likely to have to pass a mini-budget in 1997, in addition to a huge 62.5 trillion lire ($39.4 billion) package of deficit-cutting measures passed at the end of 1996.
"It is probable that with the situation we are facing we could or should have recourse to a supplementary budget, but I don't yet have the data at hand," Prodi said.
He could not be sure extra efforts would be needed until the release of official state accounts due in late February or early March, and added: "We'll see the data and then decide."
One criterion for a country to be a founding EMU member at its projected start in 1999 is to have a budget deficit which does not exceed three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Ciampi said that while the question was still open over whether an extra budget was needed, the government was ready to take further steps to meet the three percent goal.
Italy ran up a public sector deficit of 138.5 trillion lire in 1996, well ahead of a revised government target of 123 trillion, meaning the deficit was some 7.5 percent of GDP.

"Certainly, reaching the objective of a three percent ratio between the public administration deficit and gross domestic product this year is an arduous task," Ciampi told a foreign exchange conference in the country's financial capital Milan.
"We know this and for that reason we are working with determination, ready for further measures," he said.
Analysts reckon the government will have to implement a supplementary budget worth at least 20 trillion lire to keep the deficit from exceeding the limit stipulated for EMU.
The 1997 budget package leaned heavily on revenue raising measures and included a special "Euro tax" which is designed to raise 5.5 trillion lire in a one-off hike in income tax.
Bank of Italy governor Fazio, concerned at "unsatisfactory" economic growth, warned any extra budget action this year had to address spending and not resort to increased fiscal pressure.

"Rebalancing of the public deficit must be carried out, limiting growth in spending. (More taxes) would have negative effects on internal demand and on prices," he said, attending the same Milan conference as Ciampi.
Treasury Minister Ciampi said he was in agreement with the central bank governor and if an additional effort was needed, it would be on the spending side.
